mcqs.question: What is the practical test for whether an application's core is truly framework- and database-independent?
options: It has at least one interface for every class
Its unit tests take under one second to run
It uses dependency injection for every constructor argument
Its tests could run with the web framework, database driver, and cloud SDK packages uninstalled
mcqs.explanation: The defining property is that the core never references outside packages, so removing them entirely wouldn't break compilation or test execution — that's a direct, falsifiable check. Test speed, interface counts, and DI usage are common side effects, not the actual criterion.

mcqs.question: In Cockburn's hexagonal architecture, what distinguishes a driving port from a driven port?
options: Driving ports are used only in tests, driven ports only in production
Driving ports are always synchronous, driven ports always asynchronous
There's no real distinction — the terms are used interchangeably
Driving ports are called by the outside world to invoke the application; driven ports are called by the application to reach something it needs
mcqs.explanation: A driving port is the entry point the outside world uses to make the core do something, like an HTTP controller invoking a use case; a driven port is what the core calls outward for a dependency, like a repository. Sync/async and test-vs-production are not what the terms refer to.

mcqs.question: Clean Architecture's Dependency Rule says source code dependencies can only point inward. Which of the following does this rule forbid?
options: An entity class importing a type or function defined in the frameworks-and-drivers ring
A controller in the interface-adapters ring calling a use case at runtime
A use case defining an interface that an outer-ring class implements
Two use cases in the same ring calling each other
mcqs.explanation: The rule forbids an inner ring naming anything in an outer ring at the source-code level — an entity importing a framework type violates it directly. Runtime calls from outer to inner, an inner ring defining an interface for an outer implementation, and same-ring calls are all consistent with the rule.

mcqs.question: Hexagonal architecture, Onion Architecture, and Clean Architecture were proposed by different authors with different diagrams. What do they fundamentally agree on?
options: All three require exactly four named layers
An inner, dependency-free core surrounded by outer 'detail' code, with dependencies pointing inward only
They only apply to microservice-based systems, not monoliths
The core must always be implemented as an object-oriented class hierarchy
mcqs.explanation: All three styles share the same substance — a dependency-free core, outer layers holding frameworks and infrastructure, and strictly inward-pointing dependencies — while differing mainly in naming and shape. None mandates a specific layer count, a deployment topology, or an OO-only implementation.

mcqs.question: Clean Architecture calls the outermost ring 'frameworks and drivers,' treating the web framework and database as 'details.' What is this meant to convey?
options: These choices don't matter for building the system and can be picked arbitrarily
Frameworks and databases should always be replaced with custom in-house code
Only the outermost ring needs to be well-tested; inner rings don't need tests
The business logic's design and testability shouldn't depend on which specific framework or database is chosen
mcqs.explanation: Calling them 'details' is about where they belong architecturally, not about their real-world importance — the goal is that core business logic can be understood and tested without naming any specific vendor. It's not an argument against using frameworks, nor about which ring deserves testing.

mcqs.question: A use case class's entire implementation is `repository.save(mapper.toEntity(request))`, with no other logic. What does this suggest?
options: This is a well-formed use case and the pattern is working as intended
The full ring ceremony is likely being over-applied to logic simple enough not to need it
The repository interface is missing a method
The entity class should be merged into the use case for simplicity
mcqs.explanation: A use case with zero actual business rule to orchestrate is the classic sign of over-applying Clean Architecture's structure to plain CRUD — the ceremony (interfaces, mapping, a use case class) exists with nothing worth protecting from the framework. It's a right-sizing problem, not a missing method or a merge fix.
